messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out\_min} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (settled mean)
        *   $V_{out\_max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (peak)
        *   Ripple $\le 0.05\text{ V}$ (peak-to-peak)
        *   Startup $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (time to 1.8V)
        *   Settled $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (stability)
    *   Piezo: Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25nF) and $20\text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   Open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} = \frac{I_p}{2\pi f C_p} \approx 3.2\text{ V}$ (S1).
    *   Load varies: $150\text{ k}\Omega$ (S2) to $2200\text{ k}\Omega$ (S3).
    *   Reference Design (FBR): Failed on S2 (too low voltage), S3 (too high voltage/ripple), S4 (too low voltage), S5 (settling).

    *   FBR is a simple rectifier. It doesn't handle the impedance mismatch or the high-voltage excursions of the piezo well.
    *   S2/S4 failures (low $V_{out}$) suggest the need for better energy extraction or a boost mechanism.
    *   S3 failure (high $V_{out}$) suggests the need for voltage regulation/clamping.

    *   **SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):** This is the gold standard for piezo energy harvesting. It flips the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks, effectively increasing the harvested energy and allowing better control over the output voltage.
    *   **Parallel-SSHI:** Flip the $C_p$ voltage using an inductor.
    *   **Series-SSHI:** Similar, but the inductor is in series with the rectifier.
    *   **Voltage Regulation:** A Zener diode (DZ33) can prevent $V_{out}$ from exceeding 3.6V (though 3.3V Zener is close to the limit). A capacitor is needed for ripple reduction.

    *   *Topology 1: SSHI (Parallel)*
        *   Piezo terminals: `pzp`, `pzn`.
        *   Full bridge rectifier: `D1` (pzp->out), `D2` (pzn->out), `D3` (0->pzp), `D4` (0->pzn).
        *   Wait, the standard SSHI typically uses a switch and an inductor to flip the capacitor voltage.
        *   Simplified Parallel-SSHI: Rectifier to charge `out`. An inductor $L$ and switch $S$ across the piezo to flip $V_{Cp}$.
        *   Actually, a more robust approach for this specific set of constraints (especially the low $V_{out}$ in S2/S4) is to use the "Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction" (SECE) or a modified SSHI. Let's try a simple SSHI variant.

    *   *Topology 2: Bridge + Zener Clamp + Large Cap*
        *   Since the reference FBR failed mostly on S2/S4 (low power) and S3 (overvoltage), we might just need a more efficient rectifier or a clamping mechanism. But FBR is already the most efficient passive rectifier. The issue is the open-circuit voltage is too low for some loads.
        *   Actually, let's look at the "S3 failure: $V_{max} = 5.72\text{V}$". A Zener $DZ33$ would clamp this.
        *   But S2 and S4 need *more* voltage. $V_{oc}$ is $\sim 3.2\text{V}$. A bridge rectifier has $\sim 0.5\text{V}$ drop. $3.2 - 0.5 = 2.7\text{V}$. Why did S2 fail ($1.76\text{V}$)? Because of the load $R_L=150\text{k}\Omega$ pulling it down. We need a way to step up or extract more energy.

    *   *Topology 3: SSHI with an inductor and switch.*
        *   Let's use a parallel-SSHI configuration.
        *   Components:
            *   Full bridge: `D1(pzp, out)`, `D2(pzn, out)`, `D3(0, pzp)`, `D4(0, pzn)`.
            *   Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo to invert the charge.
            *   `L1(pzp, n1)`, `S1(n1, pzn)`.
            *   Controller `G1` triggers $S1$ at peaks.
            *   Storage capacitor $C_{out}$ at `out`.

    *   *Wait, let's refine the SSHI:*
        A classic parallel-SSHI:
        1. Rectifier collects energy.
        2. When $V_{pzp}$ reaches a peak, $S1$ closes, $L1$ oscillates with $C_p$, flipping $V_{pzp}$.
        3. This increases the current flowing into the rectifier.

    *   *Alternative: SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction)*
        SECE uses an inductor and a switch to transfer the entire charge of $C_p$ to $C_{out}$ regardless of $V_{out}$. This is generally more efficient than FBR for high $V_{out}$.
        1. Piezo $C_p$ charges up to $V_{oc}$.
        2. Switch $S1$ connects $pzp$ to an inductor $L1$, which then connects to `out` via a diode $D1$.
        3. This transfers charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$.

    *   *Let's try three distinct approaches:*
        1.  **Parallel-SSHI:** FBR + Inductor/Switch in parallel to the piezo. This boosts power extraction.
        2.  **SECE-like:** One switch and one inductor to transfer charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$.
        3.  **Zener-Clamped FBR:** To see if just fixing the S3 overvoltage and optimizing the capacitor helps (though it likely won't fix S2/S4). *Correction:* I'll replace this with a different SSHI variant or a Boost-converter style if possible.

    *   *Refining Proposal 1 (Parallel-SSHI):*
        *   `D1: pzp -> out`
        *   `D2: pzn -> out`
        *   `D3: 0 -> pzp`
        *   `D4: 0 -> pzn`
        *   `L1: pzp -> n1`
        *   `S1: n1 -> pzn`
        *   `G1: SYNC (ton=pi*sqrt(L*Cp), edges=both, phase=0)`
        *   `C1: out -> 0`
        *   `D5: 0 -> out` (DZ33 Zener for S3)

    *   *Refining Proposal 2 (Charge Extraction - SECE):*
        *   `S1: pzp -> n1`
        *   `L1: n1 -> n2`
        *   `D1: n2 -> out`
        *   `G1: SYNC (ton=..., edges=pos, phase=0)`
        *   `S2: pzn -> n1` (or use separate switch)
        *   Actually, a simpler SECE:
            *   `S1: pzp -> n1`, `S2: pzn -> n1`
            *   `L1: n1 -> n2`
            *   `D1: n2 -> out`
            *   `C1: out -> 0`
            *   `G1: SYNC (edges=both)` - wait, `S1` and `S2` need different triggers.
            *   Better: `S1: pzp -> n1`, `G1: edges=pos`; `S2: pzn -> n1`, `G2: edges=neg`.

    *   *Refining Proposal 3 (Half-Bridge SSHI / Simplified):*
        *   Let's try a topology that focus on the "low-voltage" failure of S2/S4.
        *   Maybe a simple SSHI but with a different switch configuration.
        *   Let's go with a "Series-SSHI" inspired structure:
            *   `L1: pzp -> n1`
            *   `S1: n1 -> out`
            *   `D1: pzp -> out`
            *   `D2: pzn -> out`
            *   `D3: 0 -> pzp`
            *   `D4: 0 -> pzn`
            *   This is getting complex. Let's stick to the Parallel-SSHI and a SECE variant.

    *   *Let's re-evaluate the Parallel-SSHI:*
        If the rectifier is `D1...D4`, and the flip circuit is `L1` and `S1` (pzp to pzn), it effectively increases the voltage across the rectifier.
        `D1(pzp, out)`, `D2(pzn, out)`, `D3(0, pzp)`, `D4(0, pzn)`.
        `L1(pzp, n1)`, `S1(n1, pzn)`, `G1(edges=both, phase=0)`.
        This should boost $V_{out}$ and energy extraction.

    *   *Wait, the Zener DZ33 is at 3.3V.*
        If $V_{out}$ reaches 3.3V, the Zener will clamp it. This should solve S3.

    *   *Let's look at the SECE again:*
        The most basic SECE is:
        - $C_p$ is connected to $S_1$.
        - $S_1$ connects to $L_1$.
        - $L_1$ connects to $D_1$ which goes to $C_{out}$.
        - $S_1$ closes at the peaks of the piezo voltage.
        - For the positive peak: $S_{pos}$ connects $pzp$ to $L_1$.
        - For the negative peak: $S_{neg}$ connects $pzn$ to $L_1$.

        Components for SECE:
        - `S1: pzp -> n1` (ctrl: G1)
        - `S2: pzn -> n1` (ctrl: G2)
        - `L1: n1 -> n2`
        - `D1: n2 -> out`
        - `G1: SYNC(edges=pos)`
        - `G2: SYNC(edges=neg)`
        - `C1: out -> 0`
        - `D2: 0 -> out` (DZ33 clamp)

    *   *Let's try a third option: a modified Bridge with a charge pump?* No, that's too many components.
        How about a "Voltage Doubler" if $V_{oc}$ is too low?
        A Dickson charge pump? No, the piezo is an AC source.
        A Greinacher circuit (voltage doubler) might work.
        `D1: pzp -> n1`
        `C1: n1 -> 0`
        `D2: pzp -> out`
        `C2: n1 -> out`
        No, that's for higher frequencies.

    *   *Let's focus on the most promising: Parallel-SSHI and SECE.*
        One more: a simple "Inductor-First" rectifier (which is basically a part of SSHI).
        `L1: pzp -> n1`
        `D1: n1 -> out`
        `D2: 0 -> n1`
        ... this is just a filter.

    *   *Let's refine the Parallel-SSHI proposal:*
        `D1: pzp -> out`, `D2: pzn -> out`, `D3: 0 -> pzp`, `D4: 0 -> pzn` (Full Bridge)
        `L1: pzp -> n1`, `S1: n1 -> pzn` (Flip circuit)
        `G1: SYNC (edges=both, phase=0)`
        `C1: out -> 0`
        `D5: 0 -> out` (DZ33 Clamp)

    *   *Wait, let's check the "S3 failure: $V_{max}=5.72\text{V}$" again.*
        If we use a DZ33 Zener clamp (`0 -> out`), $V_{out}$ will be clamped at $\sim 3.3\text{V} + \text{something small}$. This fits perfectly within $1.8\text{V} - 3.6\text{V}$.

    *   *Let's double check the components count:*
        Parallel-SSHI: 4 diodes (bridge) + 1 diode (zener) + 1 inductor + 1 switch + 1 sync + 1 capacitor = 9 components. (Limit 16).

    *   *Let's double check the SECE proposal:*
        2 switches + 2 sync + 1 inductor + 1 diode (transfer) + 1 diode (zener) + 1 capacitor = 8 components.

    *   *One more: a simple bridge with a larger cap and zener (just to see if the evolution strategy can find a better value than the reference FBR).*
        `D1: pzp -> out`, `D2: pzn -> out`, `D3: 0 -> pzp`, `D4: 0 -> pzn`
        `D5: 0 -> out` (DZ33)
        `C1: out -> 0`
        This is just FBR + Clamp. It might still fail S2/S4.

    *   *Wait, another option: the "SSH-I" with a different switch config.*
        Let's try a "Half-Bridge" with an inductor.
        `S1: pzp -> n1`, `S2: pzn -> n1`
        `L1: n1 -> out`
        This is essentially the SECE.

    *   *Let's reconsider the Parallel-SSHI's `L1` and `S1`.*
        In Parallel-SSHI, the inductor $L$ and switch $S$ are in parallel with $C_p$ to flip the voltage.
        Piezo is $C_p$ || $I_p$.
        $S$ closes, $L$ and $C_p$ resonate. $V_{Cp}$ flips from $+V_{max}$ to $-V_{max}$.
        This creates a huge current spike that the bridge rectifier can capture.

    *   *Let's organize the final proposals:*
        1. `psshi`: Parallel-SSHI (Full Bridge + Flip Circuit + Zener Clamp).
        2. `sece`: SECE (Two Switches + Inductor + Diode + Zener Clamp).
        3. `fbr_clamp`: FBR + Zener Clamp (Simple baseline to see if clamping is the only issue).

    *   *Refining `psshi`:*
        - `D1`: `pzp` to `out` (DSCH)
        - `D2`: `pzn` to `out` (DSCH)
        - `D3`: `0` to `pzp` (DSCH)
        - `D4`: `0` to `pzn` (DSCH)
        - `L1`: `pzp` to `n1`
        - `S1`: `n1` to `pzn` (ctrl: `G1`)
        - `G1`: `SYNC` (edges: `both`, phase: `0`, ton: `3e-5` - value will be optimized)
        - `C1`: `out` to `0`
        - `D5`: `0` to `out` (DZ33)

    *   *Refining `sece`:*
        - `S1`: `pzp` to `n1` (ctrl: `G1`)
        - `S2`: `pzn` to `n1` (ctrl: `G2`)
        - `L1`: `n1` to `n2`
        - `D1`: `n2` to `out` (DSCH)
        - `G1`: `SYNC` (edges: `pos`, phase: `0`)
        - `G2`: `SYNC` (edges: `neg`, phase: `0`)
        - `C1`: `out` to `0`
        - `D2`: `0` to `out` (DZ33)

    *   *Refining `fbr_clamp`:*
        - `D1`: `pzp` to `out` (DSCH)
        - `D2`: `pzn` to `out` (DSCH)
        - `D3`: `0` to `pzp` (DSCH)
        - `D4`: `0` to `pzn` (DSCH)
        - `C1`: `out` to `0`
        - `D5`: `0` to `out` (DZ33)

    *   *Wait, let me check the SECE logic again.*
        In SECE, the piezo capacitor $C_p$ is allowed to charge. Then at the peak, a switch connects $C_p$ to $L$, and the energy is transferred to $C_{out}$.
        For the positive peak, `pzp` is high. $S_1$ connects `pzp` to $L_1$. $L_1$ stores energy and then pushes it through $D_1$ to `out`.
        For the negative peak, `pzn` is high (relative to `pzp`). $S_2$ connects `pzn` to $L_1$. $L_1$ stores and pushes.
        This seems correct.

    *   *Wait, one detail on SSHI:*
        The `ton` for SSHI is typically $\pi \sqrt{L C_p} / 2$ or something similar. The optimizer will handle the exact `ton`.

    *   *Final check on constraints:*
        $V_{out\_max} = 3.6\text{V}$, $V_{out\_min} = 1.8\text{V}$.
        DZ33 clamps at $3.3\text{V}$. This is safe.
        S2/S4 fail in FBR because the load $R_L$ is too heavy for the energy harvested. SSHI/SECE significantly increase harvested energy.

    *   *Component limit:*
        `psshi`: 9 components.
        `sece`: 8 components.
        `fbr_clamp`: 6 components.
        All within 16.

    *   *S-controller limit:*
        `psshi`: 1 switch.
        `sece`: 2 switches.
        Both within 4.

    *   *SYNC limit:*
        `psshi`: 1 sync.
        `sece`: 2 sync.
        Both within 2.

    *   *Wait, the SECE `S2` needs a `G2`.*
        `G1`: `edges: "pos"`, `G2`: `edges: "neg"`.
        This is allowed (at most 2 SYNCs).

    *   *One last thought on `psshi`:*
        Should the bridge be DSCH or DSI? DSCH is low-drop, better for low power. Let's use DSCH.

    *   *Wait, the `psshi` flip circuit:*
        `L1` is from `pzp` to `n1`, `S1` is from `n1` to `pzn`.
        When `S1` closes, `L1` is in parallel with the piezo (`pzp` to `pzn`). This is the correct Parallel-SSHI topology.
